passages.happening:
‘And Elihu went on to say’ (verse 1). “Do you think this is just?” (verse 2). Job, he says, claims to be more righteous than God, and he has asked what it profits him, and what he gains by not sinning.

“Look to the heavens and see; gaze at the clouds high above you. If you sin, what do you accomplish against Him? If you multiply your transgressions, what do you do to Him? If you are righteous, what do you give Him, or what does He receive from your hand?” (verses 5-7). Wickedness and righteousness affect people like Job, not God.
passages.hearers:
This short chapter is Elihu's third speech, between his defense of God's justice and his final hymn to God's greatness. He answers two things Job has said, or that he hears Job saying: that Job is more righteous than God, and that it gains him nothing to avoid sin.

Eliphaz had made a similar point (22:2-3). Elihu uses it to answer the idea that God could be in anyone's debt. In much of the ancient world, the gods were thought to need human beings, their labor and their offerings. Elihu, like the rest of the Bible, rejects this. God is above the clouds. Human sin cannot damage him, and human goodness cannot supply a need he has.
passages.later: The Bible says that God is not indifferent all the same: ‘And the LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He was grieved in His heart’ (Genesis 6:6). And ‘The LORD is pleased with those who fear Him’ (Psalm 147:11).
passages.hard:
If God is not affected by human sin or goodness, does it matter to him how people live?

Elihu's argument could be heard as saying that God does not care, but that is not his point, and it is not what the rest of Scripture teaches. He is answering a particular claim, that Job's goodness ought to have earned him something, as though God were in Job's debt. His reply is that God cannot be put in anyone's debt. He gains nothing from human goodness and loses nothing by human sin.

The Bible as a whole holds this beside another truth. God is grieved by human sin (Genesis 6:6) and delights in those who fear him (Psalm 147:11). These are not signs of need but of love. God is not made less by human wrongdoing, yet he cares about it because it harms the people he made and the bond he intends with them. Elihu gives the first half of that picture; the rest of the Bible gives the second.
passages.asks: Elihu said that no one can put God in their debt. Ask whether you have ever served God expecting him to owe you something in return. And ask what it would mean to love him for nothing, as the accuser said Job could not.

passages.happening:
“Men cry out under great oppression; they plead for relief from the arm of the mighty” (verse 9). But no one asks where God is, the Maker ‘who gives us songs in the night’ (verse 10), who makes people wiser than the beasts and the birds.

They cry out, but God does not answer, ‘because of the pride of evil men’ (verse 12). God does not listen to empty pleas. How much less, Elihu says, when Job complains that he cannot see God and must wait for him. ‘So Job opens his mouth in vain and multiplies words without knowledge’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Elihu does not deny that oppression is real or that the oppressed cry out. Job himself described it in chapter 24. His claim is narrower: many who cry out under injustice seek escape from their suffering without seeking the God who made them.

A cry for help was a formal appeal, made to a king, a judge or a god, and a just ruler was expected to hear it. Elihu contrasts that raw cry with the prayer of someone who asks where God is. Night was a time of danger and fear in a world without artificial light, and a song in the night meant confidence given in the dark, not after the dark has passed.

His point holds for anyone: prayer can be a demand for rescue or a turning toward God. But his use of it against Job is unfair. Job has been crying to God himself, not only for relief, from the first chapter of his complaint.
passages.later: A psalm sings what Elihu describes: “The LORD decrees His loving devotion by day, and at night His song is with me as a prayer to the God of my life” (Psalm 42:8).
passages.asks: Elihu spoke of a God who gives songs in the night. Ask whether you have known a song in a dark time, and where it came from. And ask whether your prayers in trouble ask only for relief, or also for God.
